title: Mountains and Rivers Sutra
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk explores how studying Buddhism can sometimes lead to confusion and a shallow understanding of reality, rather than true insight. This is because our minds tend to focus on specific details and concepts, missing the bigger picture of interconnectedness and the present moment. To overcome this, Heigaku Talus Latona encourages us to approach spiritual teachings with humility and an open mind, embracing simplicity and freedom in order to tap into timeless awareness and find liberation.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
It's great to be back on Sunday.
I missed you all, [unclear: "organized here"].
Each summer, Red Cedar Zen community has a Mountains and Waters Wilderness Pilgrimage up to Mount Baker.
In a recent form, we spend a day at Bob Penny's farm getting prepared, then we hike up to the mountain, set up tents and stay overnight.
We spend the next full day or two up there on the mountains, and then another night on a different path home.
On the way up and on the way back, we read through, in sections, the entire Mountains and Waters fascicle that Dogen wrote.
This year, due to the wildfire smoke, we kind of got smoked out.
We ended up spending basically a retreat on the farm, studying the fascicle, waiting, hoping that the smoke would clear up on the mountain.
Aidan was able to join us for that, so that was lovely, being together.
Then we did end up doing the hike all in one day, when the air cleared on Wednesday.
Just coming out of that, like many of the sutras, every time I encounter it, I encounter something new.
When Desiree proposed doing a Dharma talk on this date, that was really fresh in my mind.
So there are a few themes in that that I'd like to explore together, and then maybe have a little conversation.
The primary translation that I'm using is by Kaz Tanahashi.
For those of you who have been able to join the weekly Dogen study group, I also miss being a part of that group.
But this gets into some of the interesting differences between the translations, and really digging in and just trying to figure out what's going on with this writing.
Another one of the major translations is by Nishijima.
Nishijima gave us the gift of numbering the stanzas, so I'll use those numbers for reference as I'm quoting out of there.
The first theme that I want to look at is basically just the message of the whole fascicle.
We'll start with the opening couple of paragraphs, where he basically presents the case.
It stands at 175, he says, Dogen presents.
This was written in the 13th century, by the way, maybe the 12th, 13th.
*Mountains and waters right now actualize the ancient Buddha expression, each abiding in its condition unfolds its full potential.
Because mountains and waters have been active since before the empty eon, they are alive at this moment.
Because they have been the self since before [unclear: "former rose"], they are emancipation actualized.
Because mountains are high and broad, their way of riding the clouds always extends from the mountains.
The wondrous power of soaring in the wind comes freely from the mountains.*
We feel something beautiful and special, most of us, when we are in the mountains.
Maybe not able to express what it is, and many of us similarly, in reading the Mountains and Waters Sutra, if nothing else, can just feel the beauty and the love that's present in it.
At the end, he presents the case again.
Around 201:
*You may think that in the mountains, many wise people and great sages are assembled.
But after entering the mountains, not a single person meets another.
There is just the vital activity of the mountains.
There is no trace of anyone having entered the mountains.*
At the end of the talk, I will come back to the beginning one that we read, the very start of it, with the translation by Brad Warner.
He was a student of the translator Nishijima.
Warner translated the whole tome in a much more casual and accessible style, while still managing to stay surprisingly true to the actual text.
He does call the Mountains and Waters Sutra the Beer and Doritos Sutra.
The last part that I just read, Warner's translation is:
*Since the distant past, great saints have lived in the mountains.
We might imagine then that the mountains must be kind of like a whole cities, chock full of saints.
But when we go into the mountains ourselves, nobody's there.
There's not even a trace of anybody having gone up there.*
While that is an important point, the part that we read earlier, "But after entering the mountains, not a single person meets another.
There is just the vital activity of the mountains," means something more to me that didn't get captured in that last sentence: not a single person meets another.
Another translation of the same section, by Nishijima, I think also captures it:
*We tend to suppose with respect to mountains in general, that countless saints and great sages might be gathered there.
After we have entered the mountains, there is not a single person to meet.
There is only the realization of the vigorous activity of the mountains.*
What I take from that is that when we are truly present with what is going on, and it's easier to do that in the mountains, the illusion of separateness between people dissolves.
Not a single person meets another because there are not separate single people.
There is only a continuous flow of interactions and relationships and processes.
Of course, we still have to step off the trail when somebody else is coming the other way.
We don't just keep on going and bump into them.

Being in the perspective of surfing the oneness of all being does not prevent us from also seeing the perspective of putting one foot in front of the other, and heaving our aching lungs up the mountain.
This often shows up as a contradiction in Zen stories.
So let's acknowledge the contradictions and move on without getting stuck in them, just as we do in life.
The vital activity of the mountains is what we are getting at here.
We could say that Dogen is using the term mountains as an allegory or an analogy.
But I think for Dogen, it's more of an example, or a type specimen.
In biology, the type specimen is like the one stuffed bird that represents the whole species.

Back before there was genetic testing to analyze it all, the scientists, the biologists, would look at their collection of birds and say, "Ah, this stuffed one, this is the one that is what I'm talking about when I say the crested northwest toad sucker."
I'm thinking for Dogen, that's what the mountains represent.
He also uses waters the same way later in the sutra.
He could talk just as well about the bricks on the path into town, or going to the toilet, as they do sometimes.
But being in the mountains, we feel something special.
For me, being in the mountains recharges me.
It's the purity that makes it easier to be in touch with what we're really reaching for in meditation.
So there I'm thinking that the mountains are kind of the type specimen for examining what's actually happening in life.
Dogen, around stanza 208:
*When you investigate the mountains thoroughly, this becomes the endeavor within the mountains.
Such mountains and waters of themselves become wise persons and sages.*
Further exploring that delusion of separateness, we investigate thoroughly.
That investigation is our practice, which gets on to Dogen's point about actualizing the fundamental point that our practice is the way of compassion, the way of Buddha.
He goes on to talk about water, stanza 206:
*Water is just the true thusness of water.
Water is water's complete characteristics.
It is not flowing.
When you investigate the flowing and non-flowing of a handful of water, thorough experience of all things is immediately actualized.*
What we are doing in meditation is investigation: watching what comes up from all sides, being completely open to every aspect of it.
This is what makes it real, according to Dogen.
We go through our lives with much of it not being real because we're not paying attention to it.
By really paying attention, that's where it exists.
That's where they're actualized.
The topic of this whole fascicle is mountains walking.

What I understand from it, letting mountains stand in for the Dharma, letting mountains stand in for encompassing all activity, and the use of the term walking, mountains walking, is the flow of causes and conditions, the infinitely complex web of relationships flowing.
Now this practice of Buddhism is intended to bring about compassion in the world.
It's not just about going off to something separate and isolating ourselves.
So how do we turn this practice of separate investigation into our life of beings together?
There's a co-worker of mine whose communication style is completely different from mine, which is very difficult for me.
This difference is not just a barrier to passing information through the communication.
It disrupts, blows my mind, disrupts my whole approach to work, so that I don't know how to prioritize, I don't know how to plan.

I'm very frequently ashamed of how I respond to them with less empathy, with less kindness, with less curiosity than I would be otherwise, because I'm responding with this additional baggage of anger and confusion.
To me, making real the activity of the mountains, enlightened activity, is the same as the process of investigating relationships and interactions.
That investigation itself, that study of myself and interactions itself, changes the narrative.
The second theme that I wanted to touch on is how entering the way broadens our ignorance.
My college chemistry teacher said that knowledge is like a sphere floating in a sea of ignorance.
The bigger the sphere of knowledge, the more contact it has with the sea of ignorance.
So the more we know, the dumber we get.
It stands at 179:
*When your understanding is shallow, you doubt the phrase "green mountains are always walking."
When your learning is immature, you are shocked by the words "flowing mountains."
Without fully understanding even the words "flowing water," you drown in small views and narrow understanding.*
What I love about that part is that section about "without fully understanding even the words flowing water."
We do read his text where he's talking about mountains flowing and get all flustered and confused: "What the heck is he talking about?"
He's saying, yeah, that's true.
But you act as if you fully understand it when I talk about flowing water, and you don't get that either.
Similarly, in the middle, about 194:
*You who call yourselves descendants of Buddha ancestors should feel ashamed of being more ignorant than an ordinary person.*
There we are.
There we go again.
We were doing fine until we started studying the Zen stuff, and now we're even more ignorant. 199:
*If you do not learn to penetrate your superficial views, you will not be free from the body and mind of an ordinary person.
Then you will not thoroughly experience the land of Buddha ancestors, or even the [unclear: "Lander Palace"] of ordinary people.*

Again, just another hit on that theme: we can talk about enlightenment, we can aspire for Satori, but we, for the most part, are not even paying attention right now to this moment, and not even fully experiencing ordinary people.
That's where the magic is.
I was thinking about it.
If I totally flub this talk, and I managed to at least pay attention to what's going on here, that would be really awesome.
That'd be totally, totally on point.
But similarly, if you don't hear a word I'm saying, don't pay attention to anything, but you manage to pay attention to what's going on there, then right on.
Good for you.
Thank you.
I'm already so tremendously flawed.
If this practice is making me more ignorant than an ordinary person, maybe I should just quit while I'm ahead.
Maybe not.
I think it's going somewhere.
I think that the world is benefiting somehow.
But we need to remember, I need to remember that humility.
The third theme that I wanted to touch on is the dualism thread.

Dogen is consistent with the Buddhist teaching about the experience of the interconnectedness of all phenomena, which argues that the separation of what we perceive is a delusion created by our upbringing and because of our nature.
That's the general teaching against getting stuck in dualism, losing track of the interconnectedness of all phenomena.
And then Dogen goes and says something like, in 181:
*Speaking of mind and speaking of essence is not agreeable to Buddha ancestors.
Seeing into mind and seeing into essence is the activity of people outside the way.*
We read that with, "Oh, oh boy, we don't want to be people outside the way."
But wait a minute.
That means that we can't talk about Dharma.
We can't talk about mind and talk about essence, because that'll make us people outside the way.
We respond by wanting to be inside the way.
But there are no people inside the way.
We talked about that earlier: upon entering the way, not a single person meets another.
So we're at that contradiction.
We're both inside and outside.
Inside the way, there is no separation of self.
We go back to it's just the activity of the mountains.

So the only way we can talk about Dharma, the only way that Dharma can be passed on from Buddha through Bodhidharma, through Dogen, is by standing outside the way and talking about it, and by practicing inside it.
So don't get caught by Dogen's baiting us.
He knows full well that it's both ways.
It reminds me of Koan 12 in the [unclear: "Muman Khan"], the Gateless Gate collection of koans.
As Robert Aitken translates:
*The priest Zhuyin called to himself every day, "Master."
And then he answered himself, "Yes."
Then he would say, "Be aware."
And he'd reply to himself, "Yes.
Don't be deceived by others."
"No, no."*
Imagine taking that out as your practice every day.
Similarly, it's very easy to be deceived by Dogen here, to be deceived by others, because he uses very dualistic terminology: people inside the way versus people outside the way.
But as he teaches, there aren't different people.
There's just the vital activity of the mountains.
Excuse me.

That koan about Zhuyin calling to himself "Master," "Don't be deceived by others," is usually interpreted as an admonition to find the truth within ourselves, rather than taking at face value what others are presenting.
And that is an important teaching.
That's one that the Buddha taught also: investigate it for yourself.
But I also interpret that koan a little differently.
It's not just an admonition to find the truth in ourselves, but a warning not to be deceived by others, as in a warning not to be deceived by the idea of others.
Coming back to that, recognizing the delusion of separateness.

Okay, so here's the core dualism thread, the core challenge that Dogen throws out in this sutra, the one that, when people read it, we usually get a little bit uncomfortable, because we're not used to reading such challenging words in Buddhism.
So as we read it, we have to ask, how do we use this to our benefit?
This is around stanza 184.
*There are careless fellows who form groups that cannot be set straight by the few true masters.
They say, "Ancient masters used expedient phrases which are beyond understanding to slash entangled vines."
Those who say this have never seen a true master, and they have no eye of understanding.
They are immature, foolish fellows, not even worth discussing.
In China, these two or three hundred years, there have been many groups of demons and six types of heretical thinkers.
People who hold this view are not even as good as shravakas of the lesser vehicles, and are more foolish than those outside the way.
They are neither lay people nor monks, neither human nor heavenly beings.
They are more stupid than animals that learn the Buddha way.*
Ouch!
Well, such criticism is the extreme of dualism, and the extreme of what he is teaching is delusion.
All this in a talk about non-self, so we must not take it just at face value.
Again and again, he reminds us to study it up, down, inside, and out.
Not long ago at work, I was the only one around when someone came from the blood bank to ask for help with the temperature in their space.
Somebody else in the facilities department had been working on it during the day, and it was still too hot in there.
So, being the only one around, I said, okay, I'll take a look.
First I went and looked at the work logs and found that the person who worked on it had been trying to make adjustments on the computer to fix the issue.
I went and looked at the computer.
It looked to me like the computer was doing exactly what it's supposed to do.
There was something going on physically out in the system, so I started walking to the mechanical room, grumbling to myself about how people are just too lazy to actually go look physically.
They just want to jump on the computer and try to fix everything.
The problem was probably that the valves were not in the right sequence.
So I walked down in the mechanical room, and I looked at the pump and shone some light into the shaft to make sure that the coupling hadn't been damaged.

I checked all the temperatures, and the temperature coming off the hot water generator was just the same as the temperature going into the pump. [unclear: "It's darn okay."] I'm not sure what the issue was.
I needed to get home, so I passed it on to the next engineer.
I said, look, this is everything I did.
I think maybe you've got to go up above the ceiling and try cleaning out some strainers.
After I got home, he texted me and said, yeah, I've done that.
I've looked at the strainers, and I'm not sure what to do next.
And I basically said, well, good luck.
About five minutes later, he texted me a picture from the entrance to the mechanical room.
You'll remember I was walking to the room while I was grumbling about the other person, thinking the problem was probably that the valves were not aligned right.
And in the picture, from the doorway, about 15 feet away, you could see very clearly that the problem was that the valves were not aligned right.
I had gotten completely into the minutiae and details without just stepping back and looking at what I thought was probably the issue.
Now, what I take from that is that sometimes we are on point and we are the masters, and sometimes we are the bald-headed rascals, as Dogen calls them.
When we read this, we hear about the careless fellows that cannot be set straight, that are even more stupid than animals, and we have to learn that it's all part of us.
And I'm okay with that.
I'm okay with recognizing, yep, I make those mistakes.
And I'm sure everybody here has gotten into that where you get so involved in the minutiae that you don't see the big picture.
The reminder is that emptiness means not that we're just hallucinating, but that we're misinterpreting this flow of causes and conditions.
We're misinterpreting the activity of the mountains.
So, by the way, where does true self fit into non-self?
I'll just leave that one hanging there for a minute.
We can come back to that.
The last of the themes that I wanted to touch on is that in the Mountains and Waters Sutra, Dogen is not teaching us something to understand, he's enticing us to approach.
I'm sorry, I don't remember exactly the quote from Fukanzazengi that we chant pretty often.
I didn't get a chance to go look that up again.
But the point is, do not suppose that what you attain becomes your knowledge and is grasped by your intellect.
Reading this [unclear: "vassal"] of Dogen's, the intent is not something that we're going to learn by reading it.
The intent is that by reading it and studying it, we are changed.
And he reveals this directly, stanza 180.
*Even if you have an eye to see mountains as grass, trees, earth, rocks, or walls, do not be confused or swayed by it.
This is not complete realization.
Even if there is a moment when you view the mountains as the seven treasures' splendor, this is not returning to the source.
Even if you understand the mountains as the realm where all Buddhas practice, this understanding is not something to be attached to.
Even if you have the highest understanding of mountains as all Buddhas' wondrous characteristics, the truth is not only this.
These are conditioned views.
This is not the understanding of Buddha ancestors.
But merely looking through a bamboo pipe at a corner of the sky.*
Go through that one again briefly.
*Even if you have an eye to see mountains as grass, trees, earth, rocks, or walls, do not be confused or swayed by it.*
So there's that first initial step we were talking about, paying attention to what's right in front of us.
Really paying attention, really studying it.
You could practice that for lifetimes and finally get to see the mountains, the grass, the trees, the earth, and the rocks and walls as they really are.
And he says, okay, you've attained that.
Don't be confused or swayed by it.
This is not complete realization.
Okay, there's something more.
*Even if there is a moment when you view the mountains as the seven treasures' splendor.*
Of course, he's not just talking about mountains.
He's talking about all of our life.
We're sitting in meditation, and we have this amazing experience.
He says, this is not returning to the source.
Meaning this is not coming back to the fundamental of the universe, the fundamental point.
There's more.
Keep practicing.
*Even if you understand mountains as the realm where all Buddhas practice.*

Even if you see that connection, if you directly experience the connection between the teaching of compassion, between the teaching of non-separateness, he says this understanding is not something to be attached to.
Because nothing is something to be attached to.
It all changes.
Go further.
*Even if you have the highest understanding of mountains as all Buddhas' wondrous characteristics, the truth is not only this.*
There's more.
There's always more.
Because it is the study and the practice that is our way.
We're not going to get there.
And that's fine.
*These are conditioned views.
This is not the understanding of the Buddha ancestors, but merely looking through a bamboo pipe in a corner of the sky.*
And of course, as we live our day to day, as we come across somebody else on the trail coming the other way, we have to look through a bamboo pipe at a corner of the sky.
And we still get to experience the wonder.
Recognizing the limitations of our views is how we care for sentient beings.
We set out on this path of compassion, and that's about studying ourselves.
Stanza 185, he says:
*The illogical stories mentioned by those bald-headed fellows are only illogical for them, not for Buddha ancestors.*
Now remember, that's us sometimes, those bald-headed fellows.
*Even though they do not understand, they should not neglect studying the Buddha ancestors' path of understanding.
Even if it is beyond understanding in the end, the present understanding is off the mark.*
And there he's giving us a hint that maybe everything I'm talking about is not something you're ever going to understand, because it's not possible to ever understand it.
And yet, keep trying, keep studying, because that's how we take care of people: we keep trying and we keep studying, and we practice not giving up.
Dogen is giving us the secret.
He's writing it there in code in little places.
So I try not to get caught up in the end, not to get caught up in the goal of enlightenment or understanding.
197, he says:
*The world of phenomena is not limited by up, down, or the cardinal directions.
They are tentatively designated.*
And there's a lot of other literature we could go into, and maybe we'll come back another time and spend a day talking about "tentatively designated."
That is that process of bumping into other people on the path or picking up the fork.
Because if you say it's all interconnected, I don't need to eat food, you're not going to get very far, you don't have to be able to care for human beings, right?
So we tentatively designate.
We temporarily say, all right, we'll treat the world as what I can perceive it as and do my best, but not take it too seriously, not take it as ultimate understanding.
At the end again, he comes back.
He tells us in 207:
*There are mountains hidden in treasures.
There are mountains hidden in swamps.
There are mountains hidden in the sky.
There are mountains hidden in mountains.
There are mountains hidden in hiddenness.
This is how we study.*
Ah, there's that hint again at the end: this is how we study.
So he throws at us a bunch of confusing, challenging ideas to work with.
We try to find the mountains hidden in treasures.
We try to find the mountains hidden in swamps.
We try to find the Buddha lands hidden in a flower, the mountains hidden in the sky, and the mountains hidden in mountains, and the mountains hidden in hiddenness.
This is how we study.
This is our practice: to look closely and not stop looking closely.
So how well does this connect to life?
How well do all these confusing, contradictory phrases engage with our ability to study ourselves and to engage with other beings?
I would like to have a chat about that.
But one more thing before we discuss that.
I'm going to circle back to the very beginning of the Mountains and Waters fascicle, but this time I'm going to share the opening as it was translated by Brad Warner.
Dogen's saying:
*The mountains and waters you see right now are the real forms of everything the ancient Buddhas ever said because they are just as they are.
They always measure up to their full potential.
They live in the timeless state and live in the here and now.
They're the self before the beginning of time.
They're the real form of true emancipation.
We get morality and integrity by depending on the mountains and waters because their virtue is so great.
Their freedom can even inspire us to take to the air like the wind.*
*Amen.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
